title: Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan
hook: a grammar teacher whose every lesson turns into Krishna

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mirabai's songs counted a treasure no thief can touch, one that grows when it's spent.

A grammar teacher in Bengal has a problem. His students come to learn Sanskrit grammar, and every rule he explains turns into Krishna. A verb ending? Krishna. A noun? One of Krishna's names. Tradition says this young teacher, Nimai, was known in his town of Navadvipa as a brilliant scholar and a fierce debater. Then he went on pilgrimage to Gaya, and came home unable to talk about anything else. His students, the story goes, closed their books and left. He let them go. He had found something louder than grammar.
screen: `A GRAMMAR TEACHER IN BENGAL.` → `EVERY RULE TURNS INTO KRISHNA.` → `THE STUDENTS CLOSE THEIR BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Nimai is the man remembered as Chaitanya. Back home, he and his friends began to gather at night in the courtyard of a devotee named Shrivasa, doors shut, singing God's names together. Drums, hand cymbals, one voice leading and everyone answering. That's kirtan: praise sung out loud, together, the names repeated again and again. Then the doors opened. Chaitanya's companions took the singing into the lanes of Navadvipa, a procession moving from house to house, and whoever heard it could fall in behind. At its center his tradition places one chant: Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Nothing but names, calling and calling. What's radical is how little it asks. No Sanskrit grammar, no years of study, no temple door to get through. You need a voice, or even just ears and the willingness to answer. A scholar who could out-argue his town set down the argument and picked up the drum. His followers in Bengal, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, remember him dancing as he sang, weeping, falling to the ground, his whole body caught up in the names. They also hold that he was more than a saint: Krishna himself, joined with Radha, come to taste his own love from the inside. Others honor him as a great teacher of devotion. Either way, what he gave the street was the same: a song anyone could join on the first try.
screen: `NIGHTS IN SHRIVASA'S COURTYARD.` · `THE DOORS OPEN TO THE LANES.` · `NOTHING BUT NAMES.` · then, large: `A SONG ANYONE CAN JOIN.`

segments.voice: Kirtan is a call and an answer, so let your breath do both: the out-breath is the leader's line, the in-breath is the crowd answering. If you like, hum softly on the out-breath or whisper a name that matters to you, a name of God if you pray, or just one soft sound, and keep the call and answer going, gently.
Kirtan. Praise sung aloud, God's names repeated together with drums and cymbals, which Chaitanya took out of a closed courtyard and into the street.
Your line: a song anyone can join. All it asks is a voice, or even just ears. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Gaudiya Vaishnava temples and homes, kirtan is sung with drums and hand cymbals, one voice leading and the group answering, and street processions of chanting, called nagar kirtan, still pass through towns and cities.

chat.says: Do you have to know Sanskrit or study for years to join a kirtan?
options: No, one voice leads and everyone answers; you just need a voice, or even ears.
Yes, you have to learn the grammar first so you sing the names correctly.
No, but only people born in Bengal are allowed to lead or join one.
chat.meaning: Chaitanya's kirtan asks little: one voice leads and everyone answers the names. That's why it could go out into the street.

Chaitanya.meaning: the Bengali saint remembered for bringing kirtan into the streets

Gaya.meaning: a pilgrimage town where Nimai's life turned

Shrivasa.meaning: the devotee whose courtyard held the night singing

Gaudiya Vaishnavas.meaning: Chaitanya's followers in Bengal, devoted to Krishna
